title: The Byzantine Empire
subtitle: 867–1204 · The Macedonian Recovery, Basil the Bulgar-Slayer, Manzikert and the Komnenian Restoration, to the Fourth Crusade

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: The Macedonian emperors from Basil I to Basil II, the military and civil aristocracies, Manzikert and the Komnenian emperors to the Angeloi

entries.label: Basil I
entries.hint: Basil, a peasant of Armenian descent from Macedonia who rose from the groom's stable to the court of Michael III, murdered his patron in September 867 and founded the dynasty that ruled for nearly two centuries; he repaired the city's churches, initiated the codification of law, recovered Bari and campaigned against the Paulicians and Arabs in the East, but failed to take Tephrike and lost Syracuse in 878.
entries.note: Theophanes Continuatus, Book V; Patricia Karlin-Hayter; Warren Treadgold, A History of the Byzantine State and Society (1997).

entries.label: Leo VI the Wise
entries.hint: Leo VI, a scholar who wrote sermons, hymns and a military treatise, completed the great legal compilation of the Basilika, issued 113 Novels, lost Thessaloniki to Arab raiders in 904 and was involved in the scandal of his four marriages, which led to his dispute with Patriarch Nicholas Mystikos and a breach in the church; he was succeeded by his brother Alexander and then his son Constantine VII.
entries.note: Shaun Tougher, The Reign of Leo VI (1997); Treadgold 1997.

entries.label: Constantine VII Porphyrogennetos
entries.hint: Constantine VII, born in the purple room of the palace and sidelined for more than thirty years by the regency of Nicholas Mystikos and the co-emperor Romanos Lekapenos, took power in 945 and spent the rest of his reign in learning, ceremonial and diplomacy; the books produced under his name, the Book of Ceremonies, De administrando imperio and the encyclopaedias, are the main sources for the tenth century.
entries.note: Constantine Porphyrogenitus, De administrando imperio (ed. Moravcsik and Jenkins, 1967); Anthony Kaldellis, Streams of Gold, Rivers of Blood (2017).

entries.label: Basil II the Bulgar-Slayer
entries.hint: Basil II, who came to the throne at 18 and defeated the revolts of the great generals Bardas Skleros and Bardas Phokas in 976–989 with the help of Rus troops, formed the Varangian Guard, destroyed the Bulgarian state in a war of forty years that ended in 1018, annexed Georgia's Tao and the Armenian lands, issued the land law of 996 against the dynatoi and died in 1025 with the treasury full and the empire at its greatest extent since the seventh century.
entries.note: Michael Psellos, Chronographia 1; Skylitzes; Catherine Holmes, Basil II and the Governance of Empire (2005); Paul Stephenson, The Legend of Basil the Bulgar-Slayer (2003).

entries.label: Romanos I Lekapenos
entries.hint: Romanos, an Armenian-descended admiral of peasant origin, forced his way into the palace in 919–920, married his daughter to the young Constantine VII, took the title of emperor and crowned his sons; he made peace with the Bulgars after Symeon's death in 927, sent Kourkouas to take Melitene in 934, issued laws to protect the peasants' land and was deposed by his sons in 944.
entries.note: Theophanes Continuatus; Treadgold 1997; Steven Runciman, The Emperor Romanus Lecapenus (1929).

entries.label: Nikephoros II Phokas
entries.hint: Nikephoros Phokas, who had retaken Crete in 961 after a siege of Chandax, married the empress Theophano, widow of Romanos II, and, once proclaimed emperor by the army in 963, took Cilicia, Cyprus and in 969 Antioch, increased the cost of the army and the state's taxes and was killed in his bedroom by John Tzimiskes, his nephew and co-conspirator, with the empress's aid, in December 969.
entries.note: Leo the Deacon, History; Liutprand of Cremona, Relatio de legatione Constantinopolitana; Treadgold 1997.

entries.label: John I Tzimiskes
entries.hint: John Tzimiskes, an Armenian general of the Kourkouas house, took power by the murder of Nikephoros; he expelled the Rus prince Sviatoslav from Bulgaria in 971, concluded the treaty of Dorostolon, settled Paulicians at Philippopolis, campaigned in Syria and Palestine in 975 as far as Tiberias and Caesarea and died, perhaps poisoned, in January 976.
entries.note: Leo the Deacon; John Skylitzes, Synopsis Historion; Treadgold 1997.

entries.label: Zoe, Theodora and the later Macedonians
entries.hint: Basil's nieces Zoe and Theodora, the last of the dynasty, gave the throne by marriage and adoption to Romanos III Argyros (1028), Michael IV the Paphlagonian (1034), Michael V (1041), Constantine IX Monomachos (1042–1055) and Michael VI (1056); the court's expenditures, the debasement of the coinage, the reduction of the army and the growth of the civil bureaucracy marked these years, described by Psellos, who served three of the emperors.
entries.note: Psellos, Chronographia 2–6; Treadgold 1997; Kaldellis 2017.

entries.label: Isaac I and Romanos IV Diogenes
entries.hint: Isaac Komnenos, who rose with the eastern army in 1057, resigned in 1059 and was succeeded by Constantine X Doukas (1059–1067), whose government cut the army; Romanos IV Diogenes, a soldier married to the widowed empress Eudokia, led the campaign that ended at Manzikert in August 1071, was captured by Alp Arslan and freed on terms, and was blinded after a civil war, dying in 1072.
entries.note: Psellos, Chronographia 7; Attaleiates, History; Treadgold 1997.

entries.label: Alexios I Komnenos
entries.hint: Alexios Komnenos, a general who seized the throne in April 1081 with the support of his family and the Doukai at a time when the empire had lost Anatolia to the Turks and faced Robert Guiscard's Normans, built a clan-based government, defeated the Normans with Venetian aid, the Pechenegs at Levounion in 1091 and the Turks with the Crusaders' help in 1097–1098, and restored the empire's frontiers in Anatolia and the Balkans.
entries.note: Anna Komnene, The Alexiad; Peter Frankopan, The First Crusade (2012); Paul Magdalino, The Empire of Manuel I Komnenos (1993).

entries.label: John II and Manuel I Komnenos
entries.hint: John II Komnenos, called the Good, strengthened the army and recovered western Anatolia from the Turks, reached Antioch in 1137 and imposed the emperor's suzerainty on the crusader states; Manuel I (1143–1180), who combined an ambitious foreign policy in Italy, Hungary and the Holy Land with a splendid court, saw the empire reach a peak of influence and then lose a great part of its army at Myriokephalon in 1176.
entries.note: Niketas Choniates, Historia; John Kinnamos, Deeds of John and Manuel Comnenus; Magdalino 1993.

entries.label: Andronikos I and the Angeloi
entries.hint: Andronikos I Komnenos, a cousin of Manuel, took power in the coup of 1182–1183, killed the child emperor Alexios II, ruled by terror and was lynched by the crowd in September 1185; he was succeeded by Isaac II Angelos (1185–1195), who was overthrown by his brother Alexios III, and the dynasty's weakness, the loss of Bulgaria and Cyprus and the Fourth Crusade followed.
entries.note: Niketas Choniates; Charles Brand, Byzantium Confronts the West 1180–1204 (1968); Magdalino 1993.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The reconquests of Crete, Cilicia and Antioch, Kleidion and the end of Bulgaria, the Normans and Manzikert, the First Crusade, Myriokephalon and 1204

entries.label: The wars with Symeon of Bulgaria
entries.hint: Symeon, a ruler educated in Constantinople, fought Byzantium for three decades, defeated the army at Boulgarophygon in 896 and at Anchialos in 917, besieged Constantinople in 913 and 924 and took the title of tsar of the Bulgars and Romans; his death in 927 opened a period of peace and a marriage alliance.
entries.note: Skylitzes; Nicholas Mystikos, Letters; John Fine, The Early Medieval Balkans (1983); Runciman, A History of the First Bulgarian Empire (1930).

entries.label: The reconquest of Crete and Cilicia
entries.hint: Nikephoros Phokas took Chandax (Heraklion) in March 961 after a long siege, ending the Cretan emirate of 828 and a century of raids on the Aegean, and in 964–965 his brother Leo and the emperor took Tarsus and Mopsuestia and Cyprus; the conquests opened the way to Syria and the Muslims' flight from Cilicia.
entries.note: Leo the Deacon 1; Skylitzes; Treadgold 1997; Kaldellis 2017.

entries.label: The recovery of Antioch and northern Syria
entries.hint: In October 969 Nikephoros's generals took Antioch, the largest city of northern Syria and a patriarchate of the Greek church, after a siege; the emirate of Aleppo became a tributary, and John Tzimiskes in 974–975 marched in a great campaign through Lebanon and Galilee that took Baalbek, Beirut and Tiberias, a short-lived advance that alarmed the Fatimids.
entries.note: Yahya of Antioch, Chronicle; Leo the Deacon; Skylitzes; Marius Canard, Histoire de la dynastie des H'amdanides (1951).

entries.label: Kleidion and the end of the Bulgarian state
entries.hint: After years of campaigning, Basil II took in July 1014 the Bulgarian army at the pass of Kleidion in the Belasica mountains, where according to Skylitzes he blinded some 15,000 prisoners, leaving one man in each hundred with one eye to lead them home; tsar Samuel died of shock, and after four more years of fighting the Bulgarian nobles submitted in 1018 and Bulgaria became a province.
entries.note: Skylitzes, Synopsis Historion 16; Stephenson 2003; Fine 1983.

entries.label: The Normans in southern Italy
entries.hint: Norman adventurers who had come as mercenaries made themselves masters of Apulia and Calabria in the 1040s and 1050s, defeating Pope Leo IX at Civitate in 1053, and Robert Guiscard took Reggio in 1060 and Bari in April 1071, ending the empire's rule in Italy after five centuries; his next target was the Balkans.
entries.note: Anna Komnene 1; William of Apulia, Gesta Roberti Wiscardi; Graham Loud, The Age of Robert Guiscard (2000).

entries.label: Manzikert
entries.hint: The army of Romanos IV Diogenes, some 40,000 to 70,000 men, was routed north of Lake Van by the Seljuk sultan Alp Arslan, partly through the treachery of the Doukas faction in the rear, and the emperor was captured and released in a few days; the defeat was not a catastrophe in itself, but the civil war that followed opened Anatolia to Turkmen bands and the Seljuk principality of Rum, and became a central event of memory.
entries.note: Attaleiates, History; Psellos 7; Carole Hillenbrand, Turkish Myth and Muslim Symbol: The Battle of Manzikert (2007); Alexander Beihammer, Byzantium and the Emergence of Muslim-Turkish Anatolia (2017).

entries.label: The Norman invasion of Epirus and Dyrrachion
entries.hint: Robert Guiscard landed in Epirus with some 15,000 men in 1081 and defeated Alexios Komnenos before Dyrrachion in October, taking the city in 1082 and advancing into Macedonia; the emperor's war chest was filled with church plate, Venetian aid was bought by the chrysobull of 1082 and, after Guiscard's death in 1085, the Norman threat subsided.
entries.note: Anna Komnene 4–6; Loud 2000; Jonathan Harris, Byzantium and the Crusades (2003).

entries.label: The First Crusade
entries.hint: After Alexios appealed to the West for mercenaries in 1095, the armies of the princes who arrived in 1096–1097 were required to swear an oath to return to the empire any lands they conquered; with Byzantine help they took Nicaea in June 1097 and won at Dorylaion, but the princes refused to return Antioch in 1098, and the crusaders' states in Syria, Palestine and Cilicia became both allies and rivals of the empire.
entries.note: Anna Komnene 10–11; Fulcher of Chartres; Frankopan 2012; Harris 2003.

entries.label: Myriokephalon
entries.hint: Manuel I's army, marching to Konya through the defile of Tzivritze (Myriokephalon) in Phrygia, was ambushed by Sultan Kilij Arslan II's army and, after a heavy loss, withdrew; the emperor had to demolish the fortifications of Dorylaion and Sublaion, a peace that Manuel called a defeat comparable to Manzikert, and the Turks gained a free hand in Anatolia.
entries.note: Niketas Choniates 7; Kinnamos; Magdalino 1993.

entries.label: The massacre of the Latins
entries.hint: After the death of Manuel I and in the regency of Maria of Antioch, in a city in which thousands of Italian merchants, Pisans, Genoese and Venetians, held privileged positions, the crowds that supported Andronikos fell on the Latin quarters in April–May 1182, killing thousands, selling thousands to the Turks as slaves and burning the churches; the memory of the event embittered relations with the West.
entries.note: Niketas Choniates 4; William of Tyre 22; Eustathios of Thessalonica, The Capture of Thessaloniki; Brand 1968.

entries.label: The Norman sack of Thessalonica
entries.hint: A Sicilian Norman army took Dyrrachion and then Thessalonica, the empire's second city, on 24 August 1185 after a short siege and killed or enslaved thousands; Eustathios, its archbishop, wrote a long account, and the Byzantine army defeated the invaders at Demetritzes a few months later, but the capture of the city was the most serious in the Balkans before 1204.
entries.note: Eustathios of Thessalonica, The Capture of Thessaloniki (trans. Jeffreys); Niketas Choniates 5; Brand 1968.

entries.label: The revolt of Asen and Peter
entries.hint: In the autumn of 1185 two Vlach boyars, the brothers Peter and Asen, proclaimed at Tarnovo the rebellion against a new tax levied for the wedding of Isaac II and, with Cuman help, restored an independent Bulgarian state, the second Bulgarian empire; the Byzantine campaigns of 1186–1187 failed and the empire acknowledged the Bulgarians' freedom in practice.
entries.note: Niketas Choniates 8; Fine, The Late Medieval Balkans (1987); Alexandru Madgearu.

entries.label: The Fourth Crusade and the sack of Constantinople
entries.hint: The crusaders, unable to pay Venice for their ships, took the Christian city of Zara for the Venetians in November 1202 and then, with the exiled prince Alexios Angelos's promises of money and church union, sailed to Constantinople in 1203; the first siege put Isaac II back on the throne and, when the promised payments failed and Alexios IV was overthrown and strangled by Mourtzouphlos in January–February 1204, the crusaders took and sacked the city on 12–13 April 1204, and a Latin empire and a Venetian share of the empire were created.
entries.note: Geoffrey de Villehardouin, La conquête de Constantinople; Robert de Clari; Niketas Choniates 10–11; Donald Queller and Thomas Madden, The Fourth Crusade (1997); Jonathan Phillips, The Fourth Crusade (2004).

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The Basilika and the Book of the Eparch, the land laws, the Komnenian system of pronoia and the privileges of Venice

entries.label: The Basilika and the Book of the Eparch
entries.hint: Basil I and Leo VI replaced Justinian's Latin law by a Greek corpus in 60 books, the Basilika, issued about 888–892, which became the standard code to the end of the empire, and the Book of the Eparch, a manual of the city prefect from about 912, listed the guilds of the capital, their rules on pricing and entry and their relations to the state.
entries.note: Basilika (ed. Scheltema and Holwerda); Book of the Eparch (ed. Koder, 1991); Tougher 1997.

entries.label: The land laws against the dynatoi
entries.hint: A series of imperial novels, of Romanos I (922, 934), Constantine VII (947), Romanos II, Nikephoros II and Basil II (996), tried to stop the great landowners buying or taking the land of poor peasants and soldiers in the villages, in the interest of the tax and military base; Basil's novel of 996 abolished the forty-year prescription in favour of the claims of the poor and made the rich liable for arrears.
entries.note: Novels of Romanos I (922, 934), Constantine VII (947), Basil II (996); Treadgold 1997; Holmes 2005.

entries.label: The Book of Ceremonies and the court
entries.hint: Constantine VII's Book of Ceremonies set out in two parts the protocol of the palace, the processions, the church festivals, the coronations and the receptions of embassies, with the precedence of officials listed in the Taktikon of Philotheos of 899; the court's rites, with their gold and silk, were meant to display the order of the world as a reflection of God's.
entries.note: Constantine Porphyrogenitus, De ceremoniis (trans. Moffatt and Tall, 2012); Philotheos, Kletorologion (899); Treadgold 1997.

entries.label: The pronoia and the Komnenian system
entries.hint: The Komnenian emperors gave the army and the administration to a ruling family circle and its connections, using titles and a new system of dignities and from the later twelfth century grants of income from state land, pronoiai, to soldiers in return for service, a form of the fief that spread under Manuel I; the system gave the empire an army and a nobility tied to the dynasty, and has been seen as the origin of the later feudalisation.
entries.note: Paul Magdalino, The Empire of Manuel I Komnenos (1993); Michael Angold, The Byzantine Empire 1025–1204 (1997); Mark Bartusis, The Late Byzantine Army (1992).

entries.label: The chrysobull for Venice
entries.hint: In return for naval help against the Normans, Alexios I granted the Venetians a chrysobull freeing their merchants from all duties throughout the empire, with a quarter on the Golden Horn and the right to trade in the main ports, a privilege that gave them an advantage over the Byzantine merchants and which later emperors, under pressure, extended and tried to cancel.
entries.note: Chrysobull of 1082 (Tafel and Thomas, Urkunden); Angold 1997; David Jacoby, ‘Venetian Commercial Expansion in the Eastern Mediterranean’ (1993).

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The conversion of the Rus, the schism of 1054, Mount Athos, Bogomils and the Holy Sepulchre

entries.label: The Bogomils
entries.hint: The Bogomils, the dualist movement founded in Bulgaria under the priest Bogomil in the reign of Tsar Peter, taught that the material world was the work of the devil and rejected church sacraments, icons and the cross; in about 1100 Alexios I had the leader Basil, a physician, burned in the Hippodrome after a trial, an event described in the Alexiad, and the movement is a source of the later Cathars of the West.
entries.note: Cosmas the Priest, Treatise against the Bogomils; Anna Komnene 15; Dmitri Obolensky, The Bogomils (1948).

entries.label: The Great Lavra of Athos
entries.hint: Athanasios the Athonite, with the support of Nikephoros Phokas, founded in 963 the Great Lavra on the southern tip of the Athos peninsula, the first large monastery of the holy mountain, which Tzimiskes' typikon of 972 organised under a protos; Athos, with its Greek, Georgian, Slavic and Amalfitan houses, became the centre of Orthodox monastic life.
entries.note: Life of Athanasios of Athos; Typikon of John Tzimiskes (972); Rosemary Morris, Monks and Laymen in Byzantium (1995).

entries.label: The baptism of the Rus
entries.hint: Prince Vladimir of Kiev, in return for 6,000 troops that Basil II needed against his rebel generals and for the hand of the emperor's sister Anna, was baptised in 988 or 989 at Cherson, took Orthodox clergy and the Greek rite home and made Rus a Christian state; its church was placed under a metropolitan sent from Constantinople.
entries.note: Russian Primary Chronicle (Laurentian text, s.a. 6496); Leo the Deacon 10; Obolensky, The Byzantine Commonwealth (1971).

entries.label: The Holy Sepulchre and the Fatimids
entries.hint: The Fatimid caliph al-Hakim ordered the destruction of the church of the Holy Sepulchre in 1009; after the treaty of 1027–1038 between the empire and the Fatimids, which included the right of Byzantine rebuilding, Constantine IX had a new church, a smaller one on the old site, completed in 1048, and the events and the pilgrim traffic form part of the background to the crusades.
entries.note: Yahya of Antioch, Chronicle; William of Tyre; Robert Ousterhout, ‘Rebuilding the Temple’, Journal of the Society of Architectural Historians 48 (1989).

entries.label: The schism of 1054
entries.hint: After Cerularius's closing of the Latin churches of the capital in 1053, the quarrel between the patriarch Michael Cerularius and the papal legate Cardinal Humbert of Silva Candida over the use of unleavened bread, the filioque and papal primacy led the legate to lay a bull of excommunication on the altar of Hagia Sophia on 16 July 1054, and the patriarch and his synod then excommunicated the legates; modern historians consider the event a dispute that became a lasting division only in the later twelfth and thirteenth centuries.
entries.note: Humbert, Bull of 16 July 1054; Anthony Siecienski, The Filioque (2010); Tia Kolbaba, Inventing Latin Heretics (2008).

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: The Macedonian Renaissance, Hosios Loukas, Nea Moni, Psellos and Anna Komnene, Digenes Akritas

entries.label: The Macedonian Renaissance and the Paris Psalter
entries.hint: The manuscripts and ivories of the tenth century, among them the Paris Psalter (Paris, BnF gr. 139) with its full-page miniatures of David in a classical landscape, the Joshua Roll and the Leo Bible, show a revival of classical figure style with personifications and landscapes taken from late antique models; the movement is called the Macedonian Renaissance.
entries.note: Paris Psalter (BnF gr. 139); Kurt Weitzmann, Byzantine Art and Culture (1951); Treadgold 1997.

entries.label: Hosios Loukas and Nea Moni
entries.hint: The monastery of Hosios Loukas in Phocis, built from the 1020s, and the Nea Moni on Chios, founded by Constantine IX in 1042–1055, have the central dome supported on squinches, a cross-in-square plan and gold mosaics of Christ and the Virgin and a cycle of the Passion that are the most complete examples of the art of the eleventh century.
entries.note: Cyril Mango, Byzantine Architecture (1976); Otto Demus, Byzantine Mosaic Decoration (1948).

entries.label: Michael Psellos and the Chronographia
entries.hint: Michael Psellos (1018–c. 1078), a civil servant and teacher at the court who served as chief minister and as philosophical master of Constantine IX, wrote in the Chronographia a lively account of fourteen emperors from Basil II to Michael VII, with psychological portraits and many references to his own role; his letters and orations, in a classical style, are a central source of the eleventh century.
entries.note: Psellos, Chronographia (trans. Sewter, 1953); Anthony Kaldellis, The Argument of Psellos's Chronographia (1999).

entries.label: Digenes Akritas
entries.hint: The Epic of Digenes Akritas, a romance in about 4,000 lines preserved in several versions, tells the story of the hero born of a Muslim emir and a Greek mother who defends the eastern frontier against raiders and the poem of a borderland where cultures meet; it is the main work of the vernacular literature of the time, and reflects the life of the frontier of the tenth century.
entries.note: Digenes Akrites (ed. and trans. Elizabeth Jeffreys, 1998); Roderick Beaton, The Medieval Greek Romance (1996).

entries.label: Anna Komnene and the Alexiad
entries.hint: Anna Komnene (1083–c. 1153), the eldest daughter of Alexios I, who had been an unsuccessful claimant to the throne and had retired to the monastery of Kecharitomene, wrote in her sixties the Alexiad in fifteen books, a classical-style Greek history of her father's reign, the principal source for the first crusade and the Norman wars, in which she presents her father as a hero and records the Latins' strange behaviour.
entries.note: Anna Komnene, The Alexiad (trans. E. R. A. Sewter, rev. Frankopan, 2009); Leonora Neville, Anna Komnene (2016).

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Constantine Porphyrogenitus and the encyclopaedias, Psellos and Italos, Eustathios and the commentators

entries.label: The encyclopaedists of Constantine VII
entries.hint: Under Constantine VII scholars compiled excerpts of ancient historians in fifty-three thematic volumes, of which only parts survive (On Embassies, On Virtues and Vices), the agricultural Geoponika and a manual of horse medicine, and the emperor himself wrote the lives of his grandfather Basil and the manual for his son, De administrando imperio; the movement is called the encyclopaedic tenth century.
entries.note: Constantine Porphyrogenitus, Excerpta historica (ed. de Boor, 1903–1910); Paul Lemerle, Byzantine Humanism (1986); Kaldellis 2017.

entries.label: John Italos and the trial of 1082
entries.hint: John Italos, a southern Italian pupil of Psellos who held the chair of philosophy, was tried by the emperor and the synod in 1082 for teaching Platonic doctrines on the soul and the pre-existence of the ideas, which the church held to be pagan; he was condemned, with eleven anathemas added to the Synodikon of Orthodoxy, and the trial was part of Alexios's wish to show his orthodoxy.
entries.note: Acts of the trial of Italos (ed. Gouillard, 1985); Anna Komnene 5; Lemerle 1986.

entries.label: Eustathios of Thessalonica and the Homeric commentary
entries.hint: Eustathios, a teacher of rhetoric in Constantinople and later archbishop of Thessalonica, wrote immense commentaries on the Iliad and Odyssey and on Dionysios Periegetes, with its learning from lost works, the best-known of the Byzantine classical scholarship, and an eyewitness account of the Norman capture of his city in 1185.
entries.note: Eustathios, Commentaries on Homer (ed. van der Valk, 1971–1987); Nigel Wilson, Scholars of Byzantium (1983).

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: The land of the dynatoi, the hyperpyron, the Italian merchants and the trade of the capital

entries.label: The commerce of the capital
entries.hint: Constantinople, with 300,000 to 400,000 people in the twelfth century, was the greatest city of Europe, with its markets, guilds and imperial workshops, its silk and its transit trade between the Black Sea, the Aegean and the Muslim world; Jewish, Italian, Rus, Bulgar and Muslim merchants had quarters, and the annual customs revenue is put by Benjamin of Tudela at some 20,000 gold pieces a day.
entries.note: Book of the Eparch; Benjamin of Tudela, Itinerary; Harvey 1989; Angold 1997.

entries.label: The great estates
entries.hint: In the tenth century the landholdings of the generals' families in Cappadocia and the monasteries of the capital grew by purchase, grant and seizure, with the legislation of the emperors against the dynatoi as the main evidence; later historians see the process as an expression of both agrarian growth and a threat to the army's recruitment.
entries.note: Treadgold 1997; Alan Harvey, Economic Expansion in the Byzantine Empire 900–1200 (1989); Angold 1997.

entries.label: The hyperpyron
entries.hint: After the debasement of the gold coinage under Constantine IX and his successors reduced the nomisma from 24 to about 8 carats by 1080, Alexios I introduced in 1092 a new gold coin, the hyperpyron, of about 20.5 carats and with a set relation to electrum and billon pieces; the coin remained the standard gold of the Mediterranean until the fourteenth century.
entries.note: Michael Hendy, Coinage and Money in the Byzantine Empire 1081–1261 (1969); Cécile Morrisson, Byzantine Money (2012).

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: Greek fire, the siege train, the Varangian axe and the great mosaics

entries.label: Greek fire in the tenth century and the siege train
entries.hint: The navy's dromons used Greek fire from pressure siphons in the battles with the Rus in 941 and with the Arabs in the Aegean, and portable hand siphons and fire grenades were developed; the army of the tenth century included wagon trains with siege engines, rams and catapults, set out in treatises of Leo VI, Nikephoros Phokas and the Sylloge Tacticorum.
entries.note: Leo VI, Taktika; Nikephoros Phokas, Praecepta militaria; John Haldon, Warfare, State and Society in the Byzantine World (1999).

entries.label: The Varangian Guard
entries.hint: The 6,000 Rus troops sent by Vladimir to Basil II in 988, who helped to win the battle of Chrysopolis in 989, formed the core of the Varangian Guard, Scandinavian and Rus heavy infantry with long-handled axes who served as the emperors' bodyguard, and after 1066 Anglo-Saxon exiles joined it; the guard was loyal to the person of the emperor and not to the state.
entries.note: Skylitzes; Psellos; Sigfús Blöndal, The Varangians of Byzantium (1978).

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: Liutprand's embassy, the Rus treaties, the Fatimids and the Venetian chrysobull

entries.label: The treaties with the Rus
entries.hint: The treaties which the Rus Primary Chronicle dates to 907, 911 and 944 and the treaty of 971 with Sviatoslav regulated the trade of the Rus in the city, with their quarter at St Mamas, the rules of their stay and the oath on the god Perun, and bound the Rus to serve the emperor in his wars; Olga's visit and baptism in about 957 was a stage on the way to the conversion.
entries.note: Russian Primary Chronicle; Constantine Porphyrogenitus, De ceremoniis 2.15; Obolensky 1971.

entries.label: Liutprand of Cremona's embassy
entries.hint: Liutprand, bishop of Cremona and the envoy of Otto I, was sent in 968 to Nikephoros Phokas to seek a Byzantine bride for the future Otto II and to negotiate over southern Italy; he was received with contempt and treated as the envoy of a barbarian king, and his Relatio, a satirical account of the visit, is the most vivid western view of the Byzantine court of the age.
entries.note: Liutprand of Cremona, Relatio de legatione Constantinopolitana; Antapodosis; Kaldellis 2017.

entries.label: The Fatimids and the Muslim world
entries.hint: The Fatimid conquest of Syria in the 970s made the caliphs of Cairo the empire's neighbours in the south, with the ten-year truces of 987 and 1001 under which Byzantine rights over the Holy Sepulchre and the protection of Christians were set out; the treaty of 1027 and the rebuilding of the Holy Sepulchre show the diplomacy of the two states.
entries.note: Yahya of Antioch; Mark Whittow, The Making of Orthodox Byzantium (1996); Harris 2003.

entries.label: The Venetian, Pisan and Genoese quarters
entries.hint: Venice's quarter on the Golden Horn was joined by Amalfi, Pisa and Genoa, which received privileges in 1111 and 1155, so that by 1170 the Italian community of some 60,000 people was a large, wealthy and unpopular body; in 1171 Manuel I imprisoned the Venetians in the empire and seized their goods, and after the war they returned.
entries.note: Treaties with Pisa (1111) and Genoa (1155); Jacoby 1993; Angold 1997; Brand 1968.

entries.label: Manuel I and the West
entries.hint: Manuel sought to restore the empire's position in Italy in alliance with the Pope and against the Normans and Frederick Barbarossa, intervened in Hungary and the Balkans and helped to cause the failure of the Second Crusade through the passage of Conrad III and Louis VII; an expedition to Ancona in 1155–1158 failed, and the policy cost the empire heavily.
entries.note: John Kinnamos; Niketas Choniates 3–6; Magdalino 1993.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The earthquakes, the movement of peoples and the cities

entries.label: The Pechenegs, Cumans and Seljuks
entries.hint: Turkic nomads from the steppes, the Pechenegs, the Uzes and the Cumans, moved across the Danube into Bulgaria and Thrace in the eleventh century, with a Pecheneg invasion that was beaten by Alexios I at Levounion in 1091, while Seljuk Turkmen began to raid Armenia and Anatolia from the 1050s; the northern frontier, which Basil II had secured, was lost to the new peoples.
entries.note: Anna Komnene 7–8; Skylitzes; Whittow 1996; Angold 1997.

entries.label: The earthquakes of 1010 and 1063
entries.hint: The earthquake of 25 October 989 caused the western arch and a part of the dome of Hagia Sophia to collapse, and the Armenian architect Trdat, the builder of the cathedral of Ani, was brought to repair it; further earthquakes in 1010 and 1063 damaged the walls and churches of the capital and of Thrace, and they are described by Skylitzes, Yahya of Antioch and Psellos.
entries.note: Skylitzes; Yahya of Antioch; Nicholas Ambraseys, Earthquakes in the Mediterranean and Middle East (2009).

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: The Porphyrogennetoi empresses, the Varangians, the Jews of Constantinople and the citizens of 1182

entries.label: The Armenians in the empire
entries.hint: Armenian generals, nobles and soldiers served in the imperial army; the annexation of Vaspurakan in 1021, Ani in 1045 and Kars in 1064 brought their lords and populations into the empire, with the Armenian Church's disputes with the Greek Church, the settlement of the nobles in Cappadocia and Cilicia and the formation of Armenian principalities there, later Cilician Armenia.
entries.note: Skylitzes; Matthew of Edessa; Whittow 1996; Nina Garsoïan, ‘The Byzantine Annexation of the Armenian Kingdoms’, in The Armenian People vol. 1 (1997).

entries.label: The Jews of Constantinople and the Empire
entries.hint: Benjamin of Tudela found about 2,500 Jews in Constantinople in about 1170, living across the Golden Horn in Pera, with tanners and silk workers among them, who had to pay an additional tax and were treated with contempt by the Greeks; communities in Thessalonica, Thebes, Corinth and Chalkis, and the Cairo Geniza letters, show a lively trade and scholarship.
entries.note: Benjamin of Tudela, Itinerary; Nicholas de Lange, Jews in Byzantium; Joshua Starr, The Jews in the Byzantine Empire (1939).

entries.label: Zoe and Theodora
entries.hint: Zoe, who inherited the throne's legitimacy as a daughter of Constantine VIII, chose and removed three husbands and an adopted son, and ruled in her own name for a few weeks with her sister Theodora in 1042 after the riot that overthrew Michael V; Theodora ruled alone from 1055 to 1056, the last of the Macedonian line, and Psellos has left a memorable portrait of the sisters.
entries.note: Psellos, Chronographia 3–6; Lynda Garland, Byzantine Empresses (1999); Judith Herrin, Unrivalled Influence (2013).

entries.label: The Latins of 1182 and the citizens
entries.hint: Choniates and Eustathios describe the artisans, traders and the poor of the capital, who resented the wealth and privileges of the Italian merchants and the taxes of the court, and whose anger fed the attack on the Latins of 1182; the same population was to suffer in the sack of 1204.
entries.note: Niketas Choniates; Brand 1968; Angold 1997.
